title: Let’s not be in denial — disenfranchisement in real
shows: A reply to Surjit Bhalla that sets the final rolls of nine states against the Technical Group's projected adults for 2026 and finds the rolls about 7 crore, or almost 12 per cent, short, with Uttar Pradesh 2.8 crore short. The authors extend the rate to about 12 crore missing voters nationally, and to about 14 crore on another analyst's estimate of the final rolls, and they say the gap includes adults who were never enrolled. They dispute Bhalla's allowance for young adults who do not register. The print edition carries a table by state.
quote: For these nine states combined, the voter list falls short of the adult population by more than 7 crore. Almost 12 per cent of the adult population is excluded.

These disenfranchised voters comprise those eligible voters who featured on the pre-SIR list and were wrongfully removed during the SIR, as well as persons who should have been added to the voter list but were not.
Even if we were to accept Bhalla’s inflated benchmark of 8.5 per cent for voluntary non-registration, there would still be 14 million unfairly excluded voters in Uttar Pradesh alone.

title: An entitled generation and an Opposition that protests too much
shows: Argues that the gap between the final rolls and the adult population mostly reflects adults who do not register, which he puts at 8.5 per cent of adults from the young missing from the 2024 roll. On that benchmark he estimates about 70 lakh eligible people kept off the rolls of Bihar and eight phase II states, and about 50 lakh in West Bengal alone. He criticises the haste of the revision and the new Form 6 declaration, and asks the Commission to publish deletions by reason, state and booth.
quote: Add a small allowance for older adults who have never registered, or who dropped off after moving, and about 8.5 per cent of adults are legitimately not on the rolls.
Allowing for the legitimate removal of non-citizens, the best estimate is that about 7 million eligible voters (range 1 to 13 million) have been excluded from the rolls without adequate explanation.

A serious opposition would demand that the ECI publish removals by reason, state and booth; that the West Bengal appeals be decided quickly; and that phase III rolls be tested against a clean roll when they are final.

title: Much Ado About (Almost) Nothing
shows: The longer version of his column. It sets out his estimate of adults, his benchmark of 8.5 per cent of adults not registering, a clean roll for each of nine states with final rolls, and a section each on Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and Assam. He puts the eligible people kept off the rolls at about 70 lakh, with a range of 10 lakh to 1.3 crore, and states which of his figures are his own calculations.
quote: Across the nine states, a clean roll would hold 535.1 million names; the final rolls hold 527.8 million, 7.3 million short.
But with only 60% of its young registered, a clean UP roll is about 85% of adults, and the final roll is within about 1.4 million of it.

“Unexplained” is not proof that every one of the 7 million was removed wrongly, and it is not small to the people concerned. But it is less than one adult in a hundred, not the one in seven implied by the headlines.
